cards.text: The writer of Lamentations is grieving over Jerusalem, which he calls the Daughter of Zion. The city lies in ruins, and right from the first line he pictures the Lord covering her with a cloud.

cards.question: The writer says the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His ___.

cards.text: He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth, and abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger. From heaven to earth, friend, that's the WHOLE way down.

cards.question: Next the Lord swallows up all the dwellings of Jacob. How does the writer say He does it?

cards.text: In His wrath He tears down the fortified cities of the Daughter of Judah, and brings her kingdom and its princes to the ground. Friend, this writer does NOT ease you in.

cards.question: In fierce anger the Lord has cut off every horn of Israel. As the enemy approaches, the writer says the Lord holds out His right hand to defend Israel.

cards.text: Then the Lord burns in Jacob like a flaming fire that consumes everything around it.

cards.question: Now the writer pictures the Lord like an enemy, with His right hand positioned. What has He done?

cards.text: Like a foe He has killed all who were pleasing to the eye. And He has poured out His wrath like fire on the tent of the Daughter of Zion.

cards.question: After swallowing up Israel and her palaces and destroying her strongholds, the Lord has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.

cards.text: Then the Lord turns on His own tabernacle. He lays it waste like a garden booth and destroys His place of meeting.

cards.question: The writer says the LORD has also made Zion forget something. What is it?
In His fierce anger, the Lord has despised the king but spared the priest.

cards.text: The Lord rejects His altar, abandons His sanctuary and hands the walls of her palaces over to the enemy. Friend, that's His OWN altar.

cards.question: Now the enemy raises a shout in the house of the LORD. What does the writer compare that shout to?

answers.text: The day of an appointed feast

cards.text: The LORD determined to destroy the wall of the Daughter of Zion and stretched out a measuring line, and He made even the ramparts and walls lament. When the WALLS are crying, friend, it's serious.

cards.question: With her gates sunk into the ground and her king exiled among the nations, the writer says the law is no more.
Even Zion's prophets are hit. What do they find from the LORD?

cards.text: The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence, with dust on their heads and sackcloth on. I know that kind of quiet, friend, from my years in the back of that junk drawer.
Then the poem says, "My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within." It grieves over the destruction of Zion's people and over the children and infants in the streets of the city.

cards.question: The poem grieves because children and infants ___ in the streets of the city.

cards.text: The children faint like the wounded in the streets, and their lives fade away in their mothers' arms. I think this one hurts, friend.

cards.question: As they faint in the streets, what do the children cry out to their mothers?

answers.text: Where is the grain and wine
When will our fathers come home
Where did all the soldiers go

cards.text: The poem turns to the Daughter of Jerusalem, searching for something to compare her to so it can console her. I don't run out of words much, friend, but this would do it.

cards.question: The poem tells the Daughter of Zion that her wound is small and will heal soon.

cards.text: The poem says her wound is as deep as the sea, and asks who could ever heal her. Then it turns to her prophets.

cards.question: What does the poem say about the visions of Zion's prophets?

answers.text: They were too hard to understand

cards.question: Zion's prophets exposed her guilt to ward off her captivity.

cards.text: Everyone who passes by hisses and shakes their head at the Daughter of Jerusalem: "Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?" Friend, that's a heckling section.

cards.question: What else do the passersby do at the Daughter of Jerusalem?

answers.text: Clap their hands at her in scorn
Bow their heads to the ground

cards.text: All her enemies open their mouths against her, hissing and gnashing their teeth: "We have swallowed her up." That's the same word used earlier for what the Lord did, friend.

cards.question: What else do Zion's enemies say about this day?

answers.text: It is the day they have waited for
It took them all by surprise
It is a day they will regret

cards.text: Then the poem says the LORD has done what He planned, overthrowing her without pity and exalting the horn of her foes. Read that one slow, friend.

cards.question: The poem says the decree the LORD accomplished was one He ordained in days of old.

cards.text: The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord, and the poem calls on the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run down like a river. Told you those walls were crying, friend.

cards.question: How long does the poem tell the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run?
The poem keeps going: cry out in the night, and pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord. What does it say to lift up to Him?
The poem says to lift up your hands to the Lord for the lives of your ___ who are fainting from hunger on every street corner.

cards.text: Then comes a prayer: "Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?" It even asks whether women should eat the infants they have nurtured.

cards.question: The prayer also asks whether priests and prophets should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord.

cards.text: Young and old lie together in the dust of the streets. And the prayer tells God plainly, friend, that He has slain them in the day of His anger.

cards.question: The prayer says the young men and maidens have fallen. By what?

cards.text: Then the prayer goes on, "You summoned my terrors on every side, as for the day of an appointed feast." There's that feast-day picture again, friend.

cards.question: In the day of the LORD's anger, a few people escaped and survived.

cards.text: The poem ends with one last line: "…my enemy has destroyed those I nurtured and reared." It's a heavy place to stop, friend, and it's okay to sit with it a minute.
